sections.title: Recognizing the species
sections.text: Russula integra (L.) Fr., the entire russula, has a fleshy cap 4–15 cm across. It is convex at first, then expands and may become slightly depressed. The surface is smooth and shiny, a little viscid in damp weather. Its highly variable colours are most often brown to yellow-brown, but may also be purplish red, greyish or, more rarely, greenish.

sections.title: Gills, stem and flesh
sections.text: The gills are thick, fragile and more or less widely spaced; they may fork near the stem. They start whitish and turn yellow as the spores mature, with paler edges. The stem is white, sometimes stained brownish, and has neither a ring nor a volva. The firm white flesh may be wine-brown just beneath the cap skin; its odour is faint and fruity, and its mild taste is reminiscent of nuts. The spore print is yellow to ochre. One published description gives subglobose to ellipsoid spores about 7.5–10 × 7–9 μm, with low warts sometimes linked by ridges; microscopic examination provides additional identification characters.

sections.title: Habitat and similar species
sections.text: It grows on the ground in montane conifer forests, especially with firs and spruces, sometimes on calcareous soils; the French source gives August to October as its fruiting season. Cap colour and a yellow spore print are not enough to identify it. Russula olivacea can share olive or wine-red tones and an ochre spore print, but often has a dull, concentrically wrinkled or cracked cap near the margin, more crowded gills and a stem often flushed pink; it grows mostly with beech, but sometimes with spruce. These are clues rather than standalone diagnoses: closely related russulas require several characters to be assessed, sometimes under a microscope.

sections.title: Edibility and caution
sections.text: Russula integra appears on the DGfM positive list; the VAPKO field guide classifies the Russula integra aggregate (R. integra agg.) as category C. That does not identify a collected specimen: russulas can be difficult to distinguish, and similar species may have a different edibility. Never eat a wild mushroom based only on a photo or this page; have it confirmed by a qualified local expert.

traits: Fleshy cap 4–15 cm across, convex then expanded and sometimes slightly depressed, smooth and shiny, a little viscid in damp weather
Highly variable colour: mostly brown or yellow-brown, sometimes purplish red or greyish, more rarely greenish
Thick, fragile, more or less widely spaced gills, sometimes forked near the stem; whitish then yellow with paler edges
White stem, sometimes brown-stained, without ring or volva; firm white flesh with faint fruity odour and mild nutty taste
Yellow to ochre spore print; subglobose to ellipsoid spores around 7.5–10 × 7–9 μm, with low warts in one published description
On the ground in montane conifer forests, especially with spruce and fir; French source gives August to October
safetyNote: The DGfM lists Russula integra as edible; the VAPKO field guide classifies the Russula integra aggregate (R. integra agg.) as category C. Russulas can be difficult to identify, and cap colour alone cannot separate similar species. Do not eat a wild mushroom based on a photo or this page; ask a qualified local expert to confirm it.
